title: Structures of sin (1987)
hook: sin can be built into systems

segments.voice: Yesterday, Laborem Exercens: people before capital, and work made for the person. Your line was the person first. Did you keep your boundary on work? Day one thousand three hundred eight.

A man at a counter needs a bed for the night. The shelter needs to see an ID. The office that issues IDs needs a home address. He has no home address; that's why he's at the shelter. The clerk is polite. The man in line behind him is patient. Nobody in the room means him any harm, and still the door stays shut, the same way, for the next person too. Something is wrong, and it isn't sitting in any one heart in that room. It's built into the way things are set up. Today's word gives that something a name: structures of sin.
screen: `NO ADDRESS, NO ID, NO BED.` → `NOBODY IN THE ROOM IS CRUEL.` → `THE WRONG IS BUILT IN.`

segments.voice: First, the name. John Paul the Second used the phrase structures of sin in a letter on social concern, Sollicitudo Rei Socialis. He meant habits, rules and arrangements in a society that keep producing harm, even when no one in particular is choosing harm today. Second, where they come from. The letter is clear that these structures don't fall from the sky. They are rooted in personal sin, and always linked to the concrete choices of people: the ones who set them up, the ones who strengthen them, and the ones who make them hard to take apart. Once built, they spread, and they become the soil for more sin. The Catechism says it in one breath: structures of sin are the expression and the effect of personal sins. Third, what feeds them. The letter names two attitudes in particular. An all-consuming desire for profit, and a thirst for power that wants to impose its will on others, both of them at any price. Neither needs a villain twirling a mustache. A lot of ordinary people quietly sharing them is enough. Fourth, an old insight with a new name. The prophet Isaiah saw it long ago, in the Douay-Rheims: "Woe to them that make wicked laws: and when they write, write injustice." Sin can be written down, filed and stamped. The teaching cuts both ways. A system doesn't excuse anyone's own choices. And being personally kind doesn't excuse ignoring the system. The letter's answer is conversion, and the solidarity from last week: a firm commitment to the good of all.
screen: `HARM BUILT INTO HOW THINGS ARE SET UP.` · `ROOTED IN PERSONAL CHOICES.` · `PROFIT AND POWER AT ANY PRICE.` · then, large: `WOE TO THEM THAT MAKE WICKED LAWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice one unjust system. Settle, and breathe. Think through a normal day: a form you filled in, a line you stood in, a price you paid, a rule at work or school. Is there one place where the setup itself keeps hurting the same kind of people, whoever happens to be on duty? Don't try to fix it in two minutes. Just see it clearly. Then ask the harder question: where am I part of it, even a little, and where could I push back? If you pray, you can bring both to God. The bell holds the time.
Structures of sin. Ways a society is set up that keep producing harm, rooted in personal choices, fed by profit and power at any price. Today's word.
Your line: sin in systems. Today, name the one system you noticed to someone else, out loud, and ask them what they see. Day one thousand three hundred eight.

howItsDone: Catholics examine structures of sin in social-justice education, in parish advocacy on laws and policies, and sometimes in examinations of conscience that ask about a person's part in unjust systems as well as personal sins.

notes: SRS §36 paraphrased: structures of sin rooted in personal sin, linked to concrete acts of individuals who introduce, consolidate and make them difficult to remove. Confirm.
SRS §37 paraphrased: all-consuming desire for profit and thirst for power, 'at any price' used unquoted. Confirm.
CCC 1869 paraphrased: structures of sin as the expression and effect of personal sins. Confirm.
The ID/address hook is an illustration, not a reported case; a Keeper may prefer a different example.
Original: 'structurae peccati' is the nominative plural; the encyclical's own Latin uses the phrase in inflected forms. Confirm spelling and church-Latin pronunciation.
'The solidarity from last week' points back to day 1298.
